pronunciation.approximation: 'TAHNG-goon' — The initial consonant is an unaspirated velar stop, closer to a soft ‘t’ than to English ‘d’; the final nasal closes the first syllable. The scholarly capital marks the name as a proper noun.

kin.label: Hanja title
kin.form: 君 (gun), Middle Chinese kjun ‘ruler, lord’ — the title element of 檀君, per the traditional analysis preserved in the Samguk Yusa.

kin.label: Mythic father
kin.form: Hwanung 桓雄, the heavenly prince who descended beneath the sandalwood tree (Samguk Yusa, Go-Dangun chapter).

kin.label: Mythic mother
kin.form: Ungnyeo, the bear-woman who endured the hundred-day trial (Samguk Yusa, Go-Dangun chapter).

pronunciation.note: Dangun is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the romanized form is plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover — only the capital distinguishes the restored form. The Korean original is written 단군 (Hangul) and 檀君 (Hanja), an attested Sino-Korean name whose ASCII form loses nothing the alphabet could have kept.

domains.title: Dangun, the Sandalwood Prince
domains.subtitle: founder of Gojoseon and first ancestor of the Korean people
domains.lead: Dangun is the legendary founder of Gojoseon and the first ancestor of the Korean people: son of the heavenly prince Hwanung and the bear-woman Ungnyeo, king of Asadal for fifteen hundred mythic years, and at last a mountain spirit watching over the land from every peak.

cards.name: Founder of Gojoseon
cards.desc: Dangun is the mythic first king whose reign marks the beginning of Korean statehood.

cards.name: Son of Hwanung and Ungnyeo
cards.desc: His birth unites heavenly descent with the transformed earth-animal, modelling cosmic and terrestrial harmony.

cards.name: Asadal
cards.desc: The sacred capital where Dangun established law, agriculture, and the ordering of the people.

cards.name: Sansin
cards.desc: After his long reign Dangun became a mountain spirit, still invoked for protection and prosperity.

symbols.name: The sandalwood tree
symbols.meaning: Dang 檀 means sandalwood; the tree marks the sacred descent place of Hwanung.

symbols.name: Bear and tiger
symbols.meaning: The two animals who underwent Hwanung's trial; the bear's perseverance became the origin of the Korean people.

symbols.name: Garlic and mugwort
symbols.meaning: The austere foods of transformation, marking the passage from animal to human and from wilderness to culture.

symbols.name: Mountain peak
symbols.meaning: The place where Dangun withdrew and continues to dwell as a protective mountain spirit.

mythology.lead: The Dangun cycle is Korea’s charter myth: a heavenly prince descends beneath a sandalwood tree, an animal bride endures a hundred days of darkness, and the first king binds law, grain, and ritual into a single realm. Its fullest early telling is Iryeon’s Samguk Yusa (1281), with a briefer notice in Kim Pusik’s Samguk Sagi (1145); shamanic and popular retellings vary the details without changing the spine.

myths.title: Hwanung Comes Down to Sin-si
myths.text: The Samguk Yusa opens the tale in heaven: the supreme lord Hwanin ruled the sky, and his son Hwanung, gazing down upon the world, begged leave to govern it and bring order to humankind. Hwanin looked and saw that the land was worth the blessing; granting his son the three heavenly seals and three thousand followers, he sent him down to the foot of the sandalwood tree, where Hwanung established the holy city of Sin-si, the ‘city of god’. There the heavenly prince taught the hundred arts: he bound the people by law, showed them how to sow the five grains, how to cure sickness with herbs, how to take husbands and wives by rite and to send the dead away by rule. The sandalwood — 檀 (dan), the tree that gives the dynasty its first syllable — stands at the center of the settlement as an axis where heaven’s bureaucracy touches the soil of earth. The myth reads like a charter: Korean civilization begins not with conquest or migration but with a delegation of heavenly order, administered patiently from a single sacred tree.

myths.title: The Bear Who Endured
myths.text: When a bear and a tiger living together prayed to Hwanung that they might become human, the heavenly prince set them an ordeal: eat only garlic and mugwort, and shut yourselves away from sunlight for one hundred days. The tiger grew restless and broke the fast before the days were out, but the bear endured to the end and was transformed into a woman — Ungnyeo, the ‘bear-woman’. She prayed beneath the sandalwood for a child, and Hwanung, moved by her devotion, took her as his wife; from their union was born Dangun, the sandalwood prince. The Samguk Yusa tells the episode with the economy of a parable: the stronger animal fails, the meeker succeeds, and a nation descends from patience rather than power. Later Korean tradition never tired of the moral — that the people’s character was shaped in a dark cave, by an animal’s willingness to endure what flesh finds unbearable, and to come out of it changed.

myths.title: Asadal and the Fifteen Hundred Years
myths.text: Dangun grew and in his day founded the state of Gojoseon, ‘Joseon of old’, establishing its capital at Asadal — a name later tradition ties to the sandalwood tree of his father’s descent and to a peak in the Taebaek range. The Samguk Yusa credits him with a reign of one thousand five hundred years, a fabulous span that marks his kingship as belonging to mythic time rather than history; the Samguk Sagi, more sober, enters the founding under 2333 BCE in the Dangi calendar that Korean tradition still counts from. The two accounts agree on the essence: Dangun gave his people law, agriculture, and ritual order, the three instruments by which a settlement becomes a state. When the sage Jizi (Gija) led five thousand followers east from the Zhou collapse, tradition says Dangun did not resist but yielded, withdrew to Jangdanggyeong, and let the new line rule — the mythic model of a succession accomplished by withdrawal rather than war, legitimacy transferred by grace.

myths.title: The King Becomes the Mountain
myths.text: The end of Dangun’s story is a retirement, not a death — at least in the older telling. Withdrawing from affairs of state after yielding to Gija, he is said to have gone into the mountains and become a sansin, a mountain spirit, one of the most beloved figures of Korean folk religion: the white-robed lord of the peak, paired with his tiger, invoked in the sansin-gut shamanic rite for the protection of villages, travelers, and the harvest. The Samguk Sagi closes its notice differently, recording that Dangun at last died and that the people mourned him for three days, giving him the honorific Wanggeom. The two endings are not rivals but layers: the chronicler preserves the king, the people preserve the god, and the mountain keeps both. In Korean sacred geography the founder never really leaves — he moves his court uphill, where every range becomes a memory of the first settlement beneath the sandalwood tree.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 檀 (dang, ‘sandalwood’) with 君 (gun, ‘prince, lord, ruler’). The sandalwood tree is the axis mundi of the founding myth; the title gun marks Dangun as the first legitimate ruler.

nameVariations.note: Hanja form used in classical texts.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Dangun, the Hangul form is 단군 and the Hanja form is 檀君. Hangul ‘단군’ and Hanja ‘檀君’, attested in the Samguk Yusa and Samguk Sagi. The ASCII form dangun is a technological compromise; the capitalized restoration Dangun is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: The Dangun myth has been read through nearly every lens available to Korean history. Confucian commentators praised the abdication to Gija as a model of virtuous transfer — the Mencian dream of rule yielded to worthier hands. Buddhist writers heard in Hwanung’s descent an echo of a bodhisattva’s compassionate coming-down, and twentieth-century nativism made the bear-woman the emblem of an indigenous line untouched by Chinese sages. Under Japanese colonial rule the story was suppressed precisely because it anchored Korean identity; after liberation it returned with force, and the new religion Daejonggyo, founded in 1909, worships Dangun as God. North and South Korea both claim him — the North stressing the excavated tomb at Pyongyang, the South the October foundation rites — while comparative folklorists note the wider northeast-Asian family of bear-ancestor tales, from the Ainu iyomante to Nivkh and Gilyak bear festivals. The interpretations conflict; the figure beneath them holds steady.
lore.culturalLegacy: Dangun is arguably the most potent name in Korean public life. Gaecheonjeol, National Foundation Day on 3 October, marks the traditional founding date with ceremonies at Chamseongdan on Ganghwa Island and Cheonjedan on Taebaeksan — altars said to mark where the founder sacrificed to heaven. His figure stands in schoolbooks, statues, films, video games, and webtoons; Daejonggyo congregations keep his rites as worship, not commemoration; and overseas Korean communities invoke him as the shared root of a divided people. The name also carries the modern tension between myth and history: the tomb ‘discovered’ near Pyongyang in 1993 is honored in the North and doubted nearly everywhere else, a reminder that founding myths are measured by what they build, not by what they bury.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Dangun is named for a tree, and the naming is the meaning. The sandalwood marks the place where heaven’s order was pegged into Korean soil; the ‘lord’ (君, gun) marks the moment an ancestor became an office. Between the two syllables sits the whole Korean claim: that the people descend from a disciplined animal and a patient god, and that their first king ruled so long his reign stops being a span and becomes a climate.

The restoration of the capitalized name is thus more than typographic courtesy. An ancestor who lives in altars, holidays, and divided nations cannot be flattened to lowercase without losing something real. Dangun is the kind of name that is a charter — and charters, unlike labels, deserve their capitals.
lore.archaeology: No artifact names Dangun, and the material record of Gojoseon is real but mute: the great Bronze Age dolmen fields of Gochang, Hwasun, and Ganghwa (UNESCO World Heritage), the walled earthworks of the northern fortresses, and the Han commandery remains at Lelang near Pyongyang, which anchor the region’s early statehood around the turn of the era. In 1993 North Korean scholars announced the excavation of Dangun’s tomb at Kangdong, near Pyongyang — a chamber with 86 ‘relics’ dated to 501 BCE — a finding honored domestically and regarded by most outside scholars as a modern construction rather than an ancient burial. The genuine artifacts of his cult are the mountain altars: Chamseongdan on Manisan, where legend says Dangun offered sacrifice to heaven, still crowns Ganghwa Island above the tidal flats, a stone witness to fifteen hundred mythic years.
